Draft. Write it down. Revise. Is the main point first? Is anything missing? Edit. Use clear words. No slang. Proofread. Check capitals, full stops and spelling. 12c81b13d98920dc.text: The $5 million comma. In the United States, a law listed some jobs. These jobs didn't get extra pay for overtime. It said: “packing for shipment or distribution”. Drivers at Oakhurst Dairy said: we don't pack anything, we just deliver. A comma was missing, so the law was not clear. A court agreed. In 2018 the company agreed to pay the drivers $5 million. One small comma changed the meaning. Think about it. What were the drivers arguing about? Why does one comma matter?

69ec05cf7a23488e.text: Get it right before you send. Nobody writes a perfect message first go — not teachers, not journalists, not CEOs. Good writers just fix it before anyone sees it. Use five steps: Plan. Who's it for? Why are you writing? Jot your main points. Draft. Get it down. Don't stop to fix things yet. Revise. Look at the big things. Is the main point first? Is anything missing? Is anything repeated? Edit. Improve the sentences. Swap slang for clear words. Split sentences that run on and on. Proofread. Check every word: capital letters, full stops, question marks, apostrophes and spelling. Spell-check helps, but it misses a lot: their/there, your/you're, off/of. The best trick is to read it out loud. If you stumble, fix that bit. Small things matter. One missing comma once helped a group of drivers win $5 million.

355dfcdd31558859.text: The $5 million comma. In Maine, in the United States, a law listed jobs that didn't get paid overtime. It included: “packing for shipment or distribution” of food. Delivery drivers at Oakhurst Dairy said they deserved overtime. Their argument was about one missing comma. Without a comma after “shipment”, the law could mean the packing of food for shipment or distribution — and the drivers didn't pack anything. They only delivered. In 2017 a court agreed the law was unclear. In 2018 the company agreed to pay the drivers $5 million. One small mark of punctuation changed the meaning — and cost millions. Think about it. What were the drivers arguing about? How can one comma change the meaning? What does this tell you about proofreading at work?
